library(edaphos)

CAU  <- ex("causal_cerrado_real_v2.rds")

> **Reproducibility.** This article is a package vignette: every number and
> figure below is computed at build time from data bundled with `edaphos`
> (`inst/extdata/*.rds`), which are in turn regenerated from public sources by
> the scripts in `data-raw/`. Nothing is transcribed by hand. Where a claim
> could not be reproduced from the shipped data, the article says so.

# Abstract {-}

Digital soil mapping (DSM) has moved well beyond regression trees, yet the
newer methods — causal inference, physics-informed and generative deep
learning, graph and quantum kernels — are rarely evaluated against each other
under a common, honest protocol, and their predictions are rarely reported
with calibrated uncertainty. We present `edaphos`, an R framework that
implements ten such method families behind a single posterior class so that
any of them can be scored with the same diagnostics, and we use it to run a
matched, spatially blocked benchmark of six methods on
`r B6$n_profiles` real World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) topsoil profiles
over the Brazilian Cerrado. The result is deflationary and, we argue, useful: a
plain ordinary-least-squares model on a directed-acyclic-graph (DAG)-selected
covariate set is the most accurate and best-calibrated method in the
comparison, and none of the five more elaborate pillars beats it on this task.
We further show, on `r CAU$n_profiles` profiles, that backdoor adjustment yields
robust *associations* with explicit sensitivity bounds rather than identified
causal effects, and that instrumenting soil carbon with a trained
foundation-model embedding produces very strong but **invalid** instruments
(first-stage *F* ≈ `r round(CAU$iv$first_stage_F)`, Sargan
*p* ≈ `r formatC(CAU$iv$sargan_p, format='e', digits=0)`) — an empirical
confirmation that a learned representation does not manufacture a valid
instrument. We conclude that the contribution of a framework like `edaphos` is
not a new best predictor but a reproducible, calibration-consistent apparatus
for asking which method helps, and for reporting honestly when none does.

# Introduction

Digital soil mapping predicts soil properties at unvisited locations from
spatially exhaustive covariates that proxy the soil-forming factors
[@McBratney2003]. The field's workhorse — the random forest and its
quantile variants — is accurate, fast and well understood, and a large recent
literature proposes to improve on it with methods borrowed from causal
inference, deep learning, and quantum machine learning. Two problems recur.
First, these methods are seldom compared under a common protocol: differences
in cross-validation scheme, ensemble budget, target transform and evaluation
metric make published gains hard to attribute to the method rather than the
harness. Second, point accuracy is reported far more often than calibrated
uncertainty, even though a soil map is used to make decisions under that
uncertainty.

A third, more conceptual problem concerns causality. It is common in DSM to
read a covariate's importance in a predictive model as evidence that it
*causes* the soil property [@Wadoux2020]. @Zhang2026causal argue that
causal inference in DSM is possible only under conditions — an explicit causal
model, causal sufficiency, and faithfulness — that observational soil data
rarely satisfy, and that the *generative*, process-informed view of causation
is the one most compatible with those conditions. Their Figure 1 illustrates,
on a global soil dataset, that the temperature–carbon association can even
reverse sign once vegetation is conditioned on (Simpson's paradox).

This article makes three contributions, all reproducible from the bundled
data:

1. a single uncertainty-calibration interface (`edaphos_posterior`) that lets
   ten method families be scored with the same diagnostics (Section 2.2);
2. a matched, spatially blocked, uncertainty-aware benchmark of six methods on
   real WoSIS Cerrado profiles (Section 3.1), whose honest conclusion is that a
   DAG-informed OLS is the strongest method here;
3. a causal analysis (Section 3.3) that reports backdoor-adjusted associations
   with Cinelli–Hazlett robustness values, demonstrates confounding directly,
   and reports a negative instrumental-variable result.

We deliberately foreground the negative findings. A framework that makes it
easy to run a dozen methods is only useful if it is equally easy to see when
they do not help.

# Materials and methods

## Data

The benchmark uses `r B6$n_profiles` WoSIS [@Batjes2024wosis] topsoil
(0–30 cm) organic-carbon profiles over the Cerrado, retrieved from the ISRIC
Web Feature Service, with covariates extracted at each profile from WorldClim
2.1 [@Fick2017worldclim], SoilGrids [@Hengl2017soilgrids] and Copernicus
fractional tree cover. The causal analysis (Section 3.3) uses a larger draw of
`r CAU$n_profiles` profiles over the same region and covariate stack. The full
retrieval and cleaning pipeline is `data-raw/causal_cerrado_real_rebuild.R`;
covariates are all open-licensed and fetched from public endpoints, so the
analysis is regenerable from profile coordinates alone.

```{r data-map, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Topsoil organic carbon (g/kg) at the WoSIS Cerrado profiles used in the causal analysis. Colour is on a square-root scale to show the long right tail."}
p <- CAU$profiles
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
cols <- hcl.colors(32, "YlOrBr", rev = TRUE)
ci <- cut(sqrt(p$soc), 32, labels = FALSE)
plot(p$lon, p$lat, pch = 19, cex = 0.35, col = cols[ci],
     xlab = "Longitude", ylab = "Latitude")
par(op)
```

## A unified posterior and calibration interface

Every predictive method in `edaphos` returns, or can be coerced to, an
`edaphos_posterior`: a small S3 object carrying a predictive sample (or mean
and standard deviation) for each target. A single function,
`uncertainty_calibrate()`, then scores any of them with the same proper and
diagnostic measures — the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), 90%
prediction-interval coverage (PICP) and mean width (MPIW), and a reliability
curve. This is what makes a like-for-like comparison across otherwise
incompatible methods possible: a random forest's quantiles, a Gibbs sampler's
draws and a diffusion model's samples are all reduced to the same currency.

## Methods compared

The benchmark compares one baseline and five frontier methods, each named by
its `edaphos` pillar:

- **P1 — OLS on a DAG-selected covariate set.** Ordinary least squares using
  only the covariates in the backdoor adjustment set of an expert pedogenetic
  DAG (Section 3.3); the baseline.
- **P4 — foundation embeddings + QRF.** A quantile random forest on the
  principal components of a MoCo-v2 contrastive encoder trained on raster
  patches.
- **P5 — quantile random forest** on the raw covariates.
- **P6 — quantum kernel ridge regression** using a ZZ-feature-map state-vector
  simulator.
- **P7 — Bayesian hierarchical spatial** model fit by a profile-MLE Gibbs
  sampler.
- **P10 — graph attention network** over a *k*-nearest-neighbour co-location
  graph of profiles.

## Evaluation protocol

All methods are evaluated on the same `r length(B6$folds)` spatially blocked
cross-validation folds (*k*-means on coordinates), on the
`r B6$response_scale` scale of organic carbon, and scored against the
*achievable* null — each fold's **training**-fold mean, never the global mean,
which would be an oracle over the rows being scored. Because ensemble size is
itself a budget, we report the ensemble each method actually used rather than
forcing equality: reading a ranking without it compares budgets, not methods.

## Causal methods

For the causal analysis we build an expert Cerrado DAG relating elevation,
climate, land cover and soil texture to topsoil carbon, and for each exposure
compute the minimal backdoor adjustment set with `causal_adjustment_set()`. We
estimate the adjusted association by ordinary least squares with a spatial
block bootstrap (500 resamples over 20 *k*-means clusters), and pair every
estimate with a Cinelli–Hazlett **robustness value** (RV)
[@CinelliHazlett2020]: the fraction of residual variance an unobserved
confounder would have to explain in *both* the exposure and the outcome to
drive the estimate to zero. Because backdoor adjustment identifies an effect
only under causal sufficiency — which @Zhang2026causal argue is seldom
achievable — we also attempt instrumental-variable (IV) estimation, using the
principal components of the foundation-model embedding as instruments for mean
annual precipitation, and test their validity with the Sargan
over-identification test.

# Results

## A DAG-informed OLS is the strongest method

Table 1 is the matched benchmark. Read it whole: the columns are accuracy
(RMSE, lower is better), variance explained against the achievable null
(NSE / R², higher is better), calibration (PICP near 0.90 is good; MPIW is
interval width), the proper score (CRPS, lower is better), and wall-clock
time.

```{r bench-table, echo = FALSE}
tb <- B6$cv_aggregate
show <- data.frame(
  Method = tb$method,
  RMSE   = fmt(tb$rmse_mean, 3),
  R2     = fmt(tb$r2_mean, 3),
  PICP90 = fmt(tb$picp90_mean, 3),
  MPIW90 = fmt(tb$mpiw90_mean, 3),
  CRPS   = fmt(tb$crps_mean, 3),
  `Time (s)` = fmt(tb$elapsed_sum, 1),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(show, align = "lrrrrrr",
  caption = sprintf("Matched cross-pillar benchmark on %s WoSIS Cerrado profiles (%s spatially blocked folds, %s scale). RMSE and CRPS lower is better; R2 and PICP near 0.90 better. Sorted by RMSE.",
                    B6$n_profiles, length(B6$folds), B6$response_scale))
```

```{r bench-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Accuracy (RMSE, x, lower better) against variance explained (R2 vs the training-fold mean, y). The DAG-informed OLS (filled) is the most accurate; every more elaborate method sits down and to the left, and three fall below the achievable null (R2 < 0)."}
tb <- B6$cv_aggregate
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(tb$rmse_mean, tb$r2_mean, type = "n",
     xlab = "RMSE (log1p g/kg, lower better)",
     ylab = expression(R^2~"vs training-fold mean"))
abline(h = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
pch <- ifelse(grepl("OLS", tb$method), 19, 21)
points(tb$rmse_mean, tb$r2_mean, pch = pch, cex = 1.6, bg = "white",
       col = "#2c3e50", lwd = 1.5)
text(tb$rmse_mean, tb$r2_mean, sub(" .*", "", tb$method), pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

Ordinary least squares on the DAG-selected covariates has the lowest RMSE
(`r fmt(min(B6$cv_aggregate$rmse_mean),3)`) and the highest R²
(`r fmt(max(B6$cv_aggregate$r2_mean),3)`), and its calibration
(PICP `r fmt(B6$cv_aggregate$picp90_mean[1],3)`) is among the best. The random
forest is a close second. The three deep or exotic methods — foundation
embeddings, graph attention, and the quantum kernel — sit progressively lower,
and all three fall **below the achievable null** (R² < 0): on these
spatially blocked folds they explain less than predicting the training mean.
The quantum kernel is both least accurate and, at
`r fmt(B6$cv_aggregate$elapsed_sum[nrow(B6$cv_aggregate)],0)` s, several hundred
times slower than the baseline. The spread among the top methods is small
relative to the fold-to-fold standard deviation
(≈ `r fmt(mean(B6$cv_aggregate$rmse_sd),2)` RMSE), so we do not over-read the
ordering beyond its headline: elaboration did not pay here.

## When both are tuned, the graph network only ties the forest

The benchmark above runs every method at fixed defaults. A fairer question for
the graph network specifically is whether, *tuned*, it beats a *tuned* forest.
Under nested cross-validation (`r GAT$n_profiles` profiles; outer folds never
used for tuning), the tuned graph attention network reaches a pooled NSE of
`r fmt(GAT$pooled$nse_vs_training_fold_mean[1],3)` against the tuned forest's
`r fmt(GAT$pooled$nse_vs_training_fold_mean[2],3)` — an edge of
`r fmt(diff(rev(GAT$pooled$nse_vs_training_fold_mean)),3)`, with a 95%
block-bootstrap confidence interval of
[`r fmt(GAT$boot_diff_ci[1],3)`, `r fmt(GAT$boot_diff_ci[2],3)`] that spans
zero (P(GAT ahead) = `r fmt(GAT$p_gat_beats_qrf,3)`). The attention mechanism is
thus, at best, *competitive* with a random forest, not superior — a consistent
but not significant difference. (We separately confirmed that the framework's
torch attention backend is not degenerate: on held-out Cerrado nodes it scores
a positive NSE competitive with both the R backend and OLS; it simply does not
win.)

## Causal inference: robust associations, and why identification is hard

Table 2 reports the backdoor-adjusted associations for four exposures, each
with its robustness value.

```{r causal-table, echo = FALSE}
e <- CAU$effects
lab <- c(wc_bio_12 = "Precipitation (per mm)", wc_bio_01 = "Temperature (per degC)",
         wc_landcover_trees = "Tree cover (per 0-1)", soilgrids_clay = "Clay (per %)")
show <- data.frame(
  Exposure = lab[e$exposure],
  `Naive beta` = fmt(e$beta_naive, 3),
  `Adjusted beta` = fmt(e$beta_adj, 3),
  `95% CI` = sprintf("[%s, %s]", fmt(e$ci_lo, 3), fmt(e$ci_hi, 3)),
  Significant = ifelse(e$signif, "yes", "no"),
  RV = fmt(e$RV, 2), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(show, align = "lrrccr",
  caption = sprintf("Backdoor-adjusted associations on %s WoSIS Cerrado profiles, in g/kg of topsoil carbon per unit exposure. RV is the Cinelli-Hazlett robustness value.", CAU$n_profiles))
```

Two associations are robust and mechanistically sensible: **precipitation** and
**clay content** both raise topsoil carbon, are statistically distinguishable
from zero, and would each need an unobserved confounder explaining ~16–18% of
residual variance in both exposure and outcome to overturn. The temperature
association carries the expected (decomposition) negative sign but is not
distinguishable from zero. The **tree-cover** row is the instructive one: its
naïve association (`r fmt(e$beta_naive[e$exposure=='wc_landcover_trees'],2)`)
all but vanishes after adjusting for climate
(`r fmt(e$beta_adj[e$exposure=='wc_landcover_trees'],2)`, interval spanning
zero, RV `r fmt(e$RV[e$exposure=='wc_landcover_trees'],3)`) — the raw signal was
largely shared climatic ancestry. This is exactly the confounding that
@Zhang2026causal warn is misread as causal, demonstrated directly on real data.

We could not reproduce the sign-*reversal* of their Figure 1 on our own global
WoSIS draw (`r CAU$simpson$global$n` profiles): with organic-carbon
*concentration* and a MODIS vegetation index the temperature–carbon slope is
negative both marginally (`r fmt(CAU$simpson$global$pooled,2)`) and within
vegetation strata (`r fmt(CAU$simpson$global$within,2)`); conditioning
attenuates but does not flip it. The reversal in their figure depends on their
specific vegetation index and carbon-*stock* construction, and we report the
attenuation we do observe rather than force a reversal the accessible data does
not show.

### A negative instrumental-variable result

Backdoor adjustment identifies an effect only under causal sufficiency.
Instrumental variables promise identification under a different assumption —
that an instrument affects the outcome *only* through the exposure. We trained
a real MoCo-v2 foundation encoder (`r CAU$encoder$channels` covariate channels,
`r format(CAU$encoder$tiles, big.mark=' ')` tiles,
`r format(CAU$encoder$epochs, big.mark=' ')` epochs on-device) and used the
principal components of its per-profile landscape embedding as instruments for
precipitation. The instruments are extremely *relevant* — a first-stage *F* of
`r round(CAU$iv$first_stage_F)`, far above the usual threshold of 10 — yet they
decisively **fail** the Sargan over-identification test
(χ²(`r CAU$iv$sargan_df`) = `r fmt(CAU$iv$sargan_stat,1)`,
*p* ≈ `r formatC(CAU$iv$sargan_p, format='e', digits=0)`). A learned landscape
representation encodes climate, terrain, soil and vegetation together, so it
reaches carbon through many paths and violates the exclusion restriction. This
is the empirical face of @Zhang2026causal's argument: even a powerful learned
representation does not manufacture a valid instrument, and IV does not rescue
identification here. We report the failed test, not a headline effect.

# Discussion

The benchmark's honest conclusion — that a DAG-informed OLS is the strongest
method, and that three of the five frontier pillars fall below the achievable
null — deserves care rather than triumphalism in either direction. It does not
show that deep learning "cannot work" in DSM; it shows that on ~1000 point
profiles with a handful of coarse covariates, the sample and signal are too
small for high-capacity models to express an advantage, and that a linear model
on well-chosen covariates is hard to beat. This is a common finding for
tabular problems at this scale, and it is precisely the kind of result that a
matched, uncertainty-aware protocol surfaces and an accuracy-only,
single-method report hides. The calibration columns make the same point from
another angle: the quantum kernel's narrow intervals (MPIW
`r fmt(B6$cv_aggregate$mpiw90_mean[nrow(B6$cv_aggregate)],2)`) buy the worst coverage
(PICP `r fmt(B6$cv_aggregate$picp90_mean[nrow(B6$cv_aggregate)],2)`), an
overconfidence that a point-accuracy table would never reveal.

The causal results carry the paper's second message. Backdoor adjustment on an
explicit DAG is a legitimate and useful tool — it recovered a robust
precipitation and clay signal and exposed the tree-cover association as mostly
confounding — but the honest object it returns is an *adjusted association with
a sensitivity bound*, not an identified causal effect. The negative IV result
sharpens this: the most tempting modern shortcut to identification, a learned
representation as instrument, is exactly the wrong tool, because the property
that makes an embedding a good predictor (it captures everything) is the
property that makes it an invalid instrument (it violates exclusion).

The limitations are inherent to the design. A single biome, ~1000–3000
profiles, and coarse covariates are a hard setting for the high-capacity
methods; a larger, denser survey with fine-resolution covariates might let the
foundation encoder or graph network express structure they cannot here, and
the framework is built to make that re-test a one-line change of data. The
benchmark scores prediction, not the process-informed *generative* modelling
that @Zhang2026causal identify as the most defensible route to causal claims;
`edaphos`'s physics-informed pillar (a pedogenetic ODE) is a step in that
direction and a natural subject for a follow-up.

# Conclusion

We have presented a reproducible framework that reduces ten families of DSM
method to a common posterior-and-calibration currency, and used it to run a
matched, honest benchmark whose lesson is deflationary: on real WoSIS Cerrado
profiles a DAG-informed ordinary-least-squares model is the most accurate and
best-calibrated method, and no more elaborate pillar beats it. The value we
claim is not a new best predictor but the apparatus — and the discipline — for
finding out which method helps, reporting calibrated uncertainty, and stating
plainly when the answer is "none of the new ones, here." The same apparatus
delivered a robust causal *association* analysis with explicit sensitivity
bounds and a clean negative instrumental-variable result, operationalising
@Zhang2026causal's caution that causal identification from observational soil
data is hard. Every figure in this article is regenerated from the bundled
data; the honest numbers are the point.

# Data and code availability {-}

`edaphos` and all bundled result data are at
<https://github.com/HugoMachadoRodrigues/edaphos>. The soil profiles are from
WoSIS (ISRIC, CC-BY-4.0); covariates are from WorldClim 2.1, SoilGrids and
Copernicus. The retrieval and analysis pipeline is in `data-raw/`
(`causal_cerrado_real_rebuild.R`, `foundation_encoder_iv.R`,
`causal_simpson_global.R`), and every benchmark figure is reproduced by this
vignette from `inst/extdata/`.
